# Software Developer - Elina Education

## Overview

**This is a doc generated by Claude based on my github commits and contributions in Elina Education repositories.**

**Full-stack Engineer, Elina Education (ElinaHub)** | April 2026 to August 2026

**Stack:** React 19, Vite, MUI, React Query, React Hook Form, Auth0, i18next | NestJS, TypeScript, MongoDB, Redis, BullMQ, LangChain, Azure OpenAI, Stripe, WebSockets

Elina Education builds a pedagogy-driven AI assistant for early childhood educators. I worked across both production codebases and owned features end to end, from data model and access control through to the interface a teacher touches. I also handled a large share of production debugging in this period.

**Scale:** 208 commits (135 containing original work), 65 pull requests merged, 498 files touched, 31 feature branches owned end to end. Roughly 36,000 lines added and 12,800 removed, excluding lockfiles and generated files.

## Some selected work

- **Product announcements system, built across the whole stack.** New backend module with audience targeting across four axes, where an empty axis means no constraint rather than no match. Read state uses two independent watermark timestamps instead of a seen-identifier list, shaped so an absent value resolves on read and no database migration was needed. On the frontend, three surfaces render through one path by design, so the preview an author sees cannot drift from what ships. Delivered in three days across both repositories.

- **Collaboration and permissions layer.** Lets teachers share learner profiles and lesson plans. Two-tier role model, five per-resource authorization guards, transitive read access through groups, and a read-only capability threaded through 38 frontend components. Existing collaborator records predated roles, and the ODM applies schema defaults on document hydration but not in aggregations, so the same legacy record read differently on different code paths. I wrote the view-only test as an explicit equality rather than a negation, which made every pre-existing record behave exactly as before with no migration, and locked the invariant with tests.

- **Fixed a structural failure in the AI retrieval pipeline.** Top-k vector search cannot answer counting or listing questions, so the assistant understated and sometimes fabricated a teacher's inventory. No prompt change fixes a retriever that was never given the data. I routed that intent class to a deterministic full-corpus renderer across 14 languages, then upgraded classification from a phrase dictionary to model tool-selection while keeping the dictionary as a fallback for provider throttling. New modes map onto an existing one deliberately, so nothing downstream changed.

- **Diagnosed a background job pipeline that accepted work and never ran it.** Nine commits of systematic instrumentation: enqueue timeout races, worker lifecycle event handlers, startup queue-state dumps. Two root causes. Staging and production shared one Redis instance under the queue library's default key prefix. And a one millisecond job delay routed work to the delayed set, where nothing promoted it. I later deleted one dispatcher I had built two weeks earlier, once the asynchronous indirection proved to cost more than it bought.

- **Cut a per-item query loop to a fixed five round trips** in the chat context builder, replacing nested per-group queries with dependency-ordered parallel waves. The same pass surfaced three unrelated bugs, including a cache invalidation that had been a silent no-op across the entire application: keys compared by identity, and a value typed as a string through a cast was actually a database identifier object.

- **Hardened authentication and session handling.** Moved tokens out of local storage across 28 files. Fixed a route guard that fought its own redirect targets. Fixed an ordering bug where a third-party identity provider failure discarded local writes that had already been reported to the client as saved, re-throwing only the one failure class that actually locks a user out.

- **Testing and documentation.** 18 backend test suites, 4,661 lines, concentrated on authorization guards and retrieval behavior, several written as regression locks for specific fixed bugs. Authored the architecture and operations documentation for both codebases, including an on-call runbook with six symptom playbooks and an authorization test plan of roughly 60 cases traceable to six named security findings.

## How I work

Backward compatibility as a requirement with a written proof, not a hope. Degradation over failure: rate-limit-aware retry that honors provider headers, and a deterministic classifier that takes over when the model provider throttles. Willingness to reverse my own work, including deleting a queue dispatcher and a polling loop I had shipped weeks earlier. I have used Claude and Github Copilot when working on both codebases.
